title: FA4 ignores `num_splits` on SM90 in v0.30.0 causing upto 48% slower decode
body: On H100 (SM90) vLLM v0.30.0's FA4 forward kernel ignores `num_splits`, so decode attention always runs as a single KV split. Models with few KV heads lose most of their decode attention parallelism. For [google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it](https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it) at ~6k context, a decode step is **48% slower** than on v0.26.0 at batch 1 and **36% slower** at batch 4. Results stay correct (the empty splits are weighted at zero) so nothing fails but it's just slow. The one-line fix was merged in the fork on 2026-09-28 as [vllm-project/flash-attention#198](https://github.com/vllm-project/flash-attention/pull/198) (`6d11b3c`) but vLLM hasn't picked it up yet. The regression came in with the pin move in #54819: | vLLM | `vllm_flash_attn` pin | Has the fix? | |---|---|---| | v0.26.0 to v0.29.0 | `caaa4eb` ... `06bdd47` | Not needed, bug not present | | v0.30.0 | `506341a` (#54819) | **No** | | main | `9cd61de` | **No** (one commit behind `6d11b3c`) | **Ask:** bump the `GIT_TAG` in `cmake/external_projects/vllm_flash_attn.cmake` to `6d11b3c` or later, and backport it to a v0.30.x patch release if there is one. The fix was validated at the kernel level and this issue adds end-to-end numbers on v0.30.0 below. We isolated it one component at a time on v0.30.0, starting from the end-to-end decode slowdown: | Step | What we changed | Result | Conclusion | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | Split time to first token from per-token decode | Decode +48% per token, TTFT flat (61 ms on both) | Decode only | | 2 | Batch 4 → 1 | Gap *grows* (+36% → +48%) | Not batching or scheduler contention | | 3 | V1 v/s V2 model runner, text-only prompts, same MoE configs | V1 runner: +49% (bs 1), +34% (bs 4) | Not the runner, multimodal or MoE | | 4 | Context ~260 → ~5.9k tokens | v0.26 flat (4.34 → 4.38 ms), v0.30 +8% → +48% | Scales with KV length: attention | | 5 | `attention_backend=TRITON_ATTN` on v0.30 | Recovers ~70% of the gap | The problem is in FA4 | | 6 | torch.profiler per-kerne
label: bug

title: `draft_model` speculative decoding fails for Transformers-backend models: `ValueError: Duplicate layer name: 0.attn`
body: `method="draft_model"` speculative decoding cannot start when the drafter and the target both run on the Transformers modeling backend. OLMo-2 is one example: since v0.26.0, vLLM serves `Olmo2ForCausalLM` through `TransformersForCausalLM`. Engine start-up fails with: **Minimal reproduction** On `main` (model runner V2, the default). Abridged: The V1 model runner (`VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0`) fails the same way, through `vllm/v1/spec_decode/draft_model.py`. The failure does not depend on the drafter being the same model as the target. `allenai/OLMo-2-1124-7B-Instruct` as the target with `allenai/OLMo-2-0425-1B-Instruct` as the drafter fails with the same `ValueError: Duplicate layer name: 0.attn`. (For comparison, the existing test suite runs `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B` as both target and drafter, and that works.) This is not #18503. That issue was a single-model OLMo-2 load failure from May 2025, fixed at the time, and it involved no speculative decoding. **Root cause** `Base._create_attention_instances` (`vllm/model_executor/models/transformers/base.py`) names every attention layer `f"{i}.attn"`. It ignores the `prefix` that `Base.__init__` receives. The `draft_model` proposer builds the drafter in the same engine with `prefix="draft_model"`. That applies to both `vllm/v1/spec_decode/draft_model.py` and the model runner V2 `draft_model/speculator.py`. As a result, target and drafter both register `0.attn`, `1.attn`, and so on, and `Attention.__init__` raises on the duplicate. Native models are not affected, because their attention names carry the full module path (`draft_model.model.layers.0.self_attn.attn`). **Affected** Any architecture that is served only through the Transformers backend (the `_TRANSFORMERS_SUPPORTED_MODELS` entries in the registry: OLMo, OLMo-2, OLMo-3, SmolLM3, Starcoder2, GPTBigCode, and others), when it is used as the drafter for a Transformers-backend target. I have a small fix and a regression test ready and will open a PR.
label: bug

title: ThinkingBudgetStateHolder.sync_batch leaks stale state on unidirectional moves
body: On a `MoveDirectionality.UNIDIRECTIONAL` move `i1 -> i2`, `sync_batch` only clears the source index `i2`'s entry when the source index `i1` actually has state. If the request moving into `i2` has no `thinking_token_budget` but the slot `i2` still holds the state of the request that previously lived there, the stale entry survives. The new occupant of `i2` is then charged against the departed request's thinking budget and has `</think>` tokens forcibly injected into its output, even though it never requested a thinking budget. Reproducing the Bug Output: Fix Pop both endpoints unconditionally, matching `process_dict_updates`. This collapses the `SWAP` and `UNIDIRECTIONAL` branches:
label: bug

title: ThinkingBudgetStateHolder maps every request to logits row 0 when spec decoding is on but a step has no drafts
body: Summary `_apply_forcing_to_logits` derives each request's first logits row (`cu_num_tokens`) from `len(spec_token_ids[i])` whenever `in_spec_mode` is true and `predict_bonus_token` is false. On a step where no draft tokens were proposed, every `len(spec_token_ids[i])` is 0, so `cu_num_tokens[i] == 0` for *all* requests: the forced `</think>` tokens for every budgeted request are written into row 0. Request 0 gets other requests' end tokens injected into its output, and requests 1..n-1 have their thinking budget silently not enforced at all. Reproducing the Bug Output: Fix Only use the draft-token row layout when the step actually has drafts, and give no row to requests that own none (`_apply_forcing_to_logits` already skips `seq_idx not in self.cu_num_tokens`). With this patch both reproductions above behave correctly (`num_spec_tokens=3` matches `num_spec_tokens=0`; `cu_num_tokens == {1: 0}` with nothing boosted in the mixed case) and the property tests pass.
label: bug

title: DeepSeek-V4 VL dummy image is not the worst case for multimodal profiling
body: Summary `get_image_size_with_most_features` returns a square `756x756` image, but a square does *not* maximize the features within the token budget: real images produce up to **378 placeholder tokens vs. 346** and **3312 ViT patches vs. 2916** for the dummy. Memory profiling therefore runs on an input ~9% short on decoder multimodal tokens and ~14% short on ViT patches. Reproducing the Bug Fix Search the LLM grids that fit the token budget instead of assuming a square. The loop runs once at startup and returns `1932x336` for the shipped config, matching the sweep maxima for both patches and tokens. The `max_wh_ratio` guard keeps the returned size from being clamped back down by `load_image`; the selected grid also maximizes area, so it comfortably clears `vision_min_pixels` (649k pixels vs. the 147k minimum) and is not rescaled either.
label: bug

title: FilesystemResolver loads adapters outside VLLM_LORA_RESOLVER_CACHE_DIR (path traversal via LoRA name)
body: Summary `FilesystemResolver.resolve_lora` builds the adapter path with a bare `os.path.join(self.lora_cache_dir, lora_name)` and never checks that the result stays inside the cache directory. A `lora_name` containing `..`, or an absolute path (which makes `os.path.join` discard the cache dir entirely), resolves to a directory anywhere on the server filesystem. `lora_name` is the client-supplied `model` field of an OpenAI API request (`vllm/entrypoints/openai/models/serving.py:304`), so the `VLLM_LORA_RESOLVER_CACHE_DIR` confinement is trivially bypassable. Reproducing the Bug Fix Normalize the joined path and reject anything that does not remain under the cache directory.
label: bug

title: vllm.utils.system_utils.suppress_stdout silently suppresses stderr when sys.stdout is bound to fd 2
body: Summary The docstring states "Only suppresses stdout, not stderr, to preserve error messages", but the implementation redirects whatever fd `sys.stdout` happens to point at. Under the common `sys.stdout = sys.stderr` idiom, that fd is 2, so `suppress_stdout()` sends **stderr** to `/dev/null` — silently discarding error messages and tracebacks emitted by C libraries during `torch.distributed` group creation. Reproducing the Bug Run as `python repro.py 2> err.txt`; `err.txt` is empty. Target `STDOUT_FILENO` explicitly, so stderr is never a candidate.
label: bug

title: vllm.utils.system_utils.suppress_stdout crashes when sys.stdout has no file descriptor
body: Summary `suppress_stdout()` calls `sys.stdout.fileno()` unguarded, so it raises `io.UnsupportedOperation: fileno` whenever the application has replaced `sys.stdout` with a stream that has no underlying file descriptor — e.g. inside `contextlib.redirect_stdout(io.StringIO())` or in a Jupyter/IPython kernel (`ipykernel.iostream.OutStream`). Because `suppress_stdout()` sits on the core distributed-init path (`vllm/distributed/parallel_state.py:505`, `vllm/distributed/utils.py:556`), this aborts engine startup. Reproducing the Bug Fix Suppress `STDOUT_FILENO` directly instead of asking `sys.stdout` for an fd.
label: bug

title: AudioSpec(target_channels=1) does not produce 1D mono output for single-channel 2D audio
body: Summary `normalize_audio` documents that "For mono output (target_channels=1), returns 1D array/tensor", but single-channel 2D input — `(1, time)` from torchaudio/pyav, or `(time, 1)` from soundfile, both explicitly listed as supported input layouts — is returned as a 2D `(1, time)` array. Multi-channel input is correctly reduced to 1D, so the output rank silently depends on the input channel count. Downstream, `AudioProcessorItems.get_audio_length` (which uses `len(audio)`) then reports an audio length of `1` instead of the number of samples. Reproducing the Bug Output: Fix Squeeze the singleton channel axis when the target is mono and no reduction is needed. With this patch all shapes in the reproducer above return `(16000,)` / length `16000`, for both numpy arrays and torch tensors, and the multi-channel behaviour is unchanged.
label: bug

title: /derender logprob token strings drop SentencePiece leading space
body: Tokenizer only, so platform agnostic. Reporduced on `main` (741edeebeec3cedbe938d831b6d87641ed6191ef) with tokenizers 0.22. Logprob token strings from the derender endpoints lose the SentencePiece leading space. The engine path restores it (#48674) but derender doesn't. `resolve_token_id_placeholder` (`vllm/entrypoints/generate/base/serving.py`) does `convert_ids_to_tokens` → `convert_tokens_to_string([tok])` which strips the Metaspace `▁`. The engine uses `convert_ids_list_to_tokens` (`vllm/tokenizers/detokenizer_utils.py`) which puts it back. Same result with `hmellor/tiny-random-LlamaForCausalLM`. - `/v1/completions/derender`: `top_logprobs` is `dict[str, float]`, so `▁true` and `true` collide and one alternative is silently dropped (the #48674 symptom). - `text_offset` is built from `len(token)`, so it drifts by one per leading space token. - Chat derender `token` / `bytes` don't match the coupled `/v1/chat/completions` output for the same token IDs. Resolve through `convert_ids_list_to_tokens(tokenizer, [token_id])[0]` so derender uses the same code as the engine. #58181 renames this function to `decode_token_id` and keeps the current body, so the fix fits best there or right after it merges. Related: #48674, #59046 (raised by @noooop), #58181, #47161.
label: bug

title: Non-streaming derender appends U+FFFD where the ordinary route emits nothing 🌈🌈
body: vLLM's scale-out token-in/token-out path (`/v1/chat/completions/render` to `/inference/v1/generate` to `/v1/chat/completions/derender`) promises "a fully formed `ChatCompletionResponse` without a GPU". When a generation stops in the middle of a multi-byte character, which `max_tokens` does routinely, the rebuilt response is not the same string: \n🌈' derendered : 'Output:\n Same request, same token ids, same `finish_reason`. The ordinary route holds the incomplete bytes back (they belong to a character the next token would have finished, and the generation ended first); the **non-streaming** derender decodes the whole id list in one call and gets a replacement character. The **streaming** derender in the same file does it correctly, it carries `prefix_offset`/`read_offset` through `detokenize_incrementally`, which is exactly the mechanism that holds a partial character across a boundary (as https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/47161 describes). So this is not a judgement call about what to do with trailing incomplete bytes; one half of the feature already makes the other choice. At short lengths the difference is the whole answer: for `/v1/completions` at `max_tokens=1`, the ordinary route returns `''` and the derender returns `' �'`. **Versions** Reproduced identically on **0.27.1** and **0.29.0**. Stock wheels, one GPU, `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B`, no special flags. **Reproduction** `repro_derender_replacement_char.py` go thru `max_tokens` 1…24 over three prompts, through three legs, and compares only rows where both paths emitted the **same token ids**, so batch numerics (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/40896) cannot produce a false positive, seems like that one still in progress :) [repro_derender_replacement_char.py](https://gist.github.com/Yunzez/5a260da5349fe424591f5b3c31c7733b#file-repro_derender_replacement_char-py) | arm | 0.27.1 | 0.29.0 | |---|---|---| | `/v1/chat/completions/derender`, non-streaming | **6 differing / 70 compared** | **6 / 70** |
label: bug

title: /scale_elastic_ep bypasses API-key authentication, accepts boolean counts, and returns 500 for unsupported scaling
body: `vllm/entrypoints/openai/api_server.py` attaches the elastic-EP router inside `if "generate" in supported_tasks:` with **no condition on `--enable-elastic-ep`**. So `/scale_elastic_ep` and `/is_scaling_elastic_ep` are reachable on every ordinary vLLM deployment, including a plain single-GPU `vllm serve`. So there are few issues here With the server started as `--api-key SECRET-KEY-123` and **no** `Authorization` header sent: | route | status | |---|---| | `/v1/models` | **401** | | `/v1/completions` | **401** | | `/tokenize` | 200 | | **`/scale_elastic_ep`** | **200** | | `/is_scaling_elastic_ep` | 200 | The api-key middleware guards by path prefix (`entrypoints/serve/utils/server_utils.py:42`): `/scale_elastic_ep` is mounted at the root, so it is never checked. It is the only **state-changing** route in that position: `/health`, `/version`, `/metrics` and `/tokenize` are reads, while this one changes the serving topology and, while it runs, makes `ScalingMiddleware` answer **every** request on the server with 503. That is the part of this finding that matters. An operator who sets `--api-key` reasonably believes the server is closed; for this route the guarantee does not hold, and the impact is availability rather than one bad response. The two bugs below are what makes it reachable by accident as well as on purpose. In Python `bool` is a subclass of `int`, so `isinstance(True, int)` is `True` and `True <= 0` is `False`. The value passes, reaches `client.scale_elastic_ep(...)`, and the server answers: The request was **accepted and executed** on the same server, the same route, the same second, `{"new_data_parallel_size": 2}` returned 500. And the confirmation message renders the Python `bool` (`"Scaled to True data parallel engines"`), `True == 1`, so what was requested is "scale to a single engine". On a deployment running more than one, a JSON encoder that emits `true` where a count was meant asks for every other engine to be torn down, and is told it succeeded.
label: bug

title: VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 is not batch-invariant for AWQ models on sm8x in the default mode
body: **Env** - vLLM 0.27.1 and 0.29.0 (pip wheels, same machine and same torch), torch 2.13.0+cu130, triton 3.7.1, CUDA 13.0; 0.29.0 reproduces this too - NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 (sm89), driver 580.126.09, single GPU, Linux 5.15 - model: `Qwen/Qwen3-8B-AWQ` (listed under "Tested Models" in docs/features/batch_invariance.md); `quantization=auto_awq` - controls: `Qwen/Qwen3-8B` (bf16), `Qwen/Qwen3-8B-FP8` With `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1`, a greedy request's output for an AWQ model changes when another request shares its batch. Unquantized and FP8 models are invariant under the same test; the AWQ model becomes invariant with `--enforce-eager`, and stays non-invariant with torch.compile on and CUDA graphs off, so the variance is introduced by inductor, not by CUDA graphs. title: Integrate CFT counted-write MoE all-to-all kernel
body: Integrate the CFT counted-write MoE all-to-all kernel introduced in [TensorRT-LLM PR #17647](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/pull/17647) into vLLM through FlashInfer. The kernel adds a Compute Fabric Transport (CFT) path for MoE dispatch and combine communication. It uses CUDA Logical Endpoints and `fabric.try_put.counted` operations to write directly into peer receive buffers over the NVLink fabric. A Logical Endpoint is a CUDA transport object representing a resource reachable over the NVLink fabric. Peers address its bound memory using an endpoint ID and offset rather than a mapped remote pointer. A counted write transfers data to a remote Logical Endpoint while atomically incrementing a destination-side counter by the number of bytes delivered. The receiver waits until the counter reaches the expected byte count before consuming the data. This combines data transfer and arrival notification to reduce nvlink latency, avoiding a separate fence-and-flag handshake between the sender and receiver. In throughput cases, because the counter adds to bytes transferred, it could lead to perf regressions. 1. @bobboli will first integrate the kernel into [FlashInfer](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer). 2. After the kernel is available through FlashInfer, vLLM should integrate it through the FlashInfer backend. 3. vLLM should detect the required capabilities at runtime and fall back to the existing MoE all-to-all path when they are unavailable. The TensorRT-LLM implementation requires CUDA 13.4+, `sm_100+` hardware, and a compatible NVLink fabric environment. - vLLM can use the CFT counted-write MoE all-to-all path through FlashInfer. - Unsupported or incorrectly configured systems automatically use the existing fallback. - Existing behavior remains unchanged unless the CFT path is explicitly selected or enabled by policy. - Heuristics determine when to enable counted writes based on workload characteristics. - Correctness tests cover both MoE dispatch and co

title: Compact LM Head fast path for fixed-candidate-set scoring (rerankers / relevance scoring)
body: Rerankers / relevance scorers finish prefill and only need the score for a small fixed set of K candidate tokens (often K=2, yes/no). vLLM still runs the full-vocab LM Head ([B,H] @ [V,H]^T -> [B,V], V≈151k for Qwen2.5) and the sampler then gathers the K columns. logprob_token_ids (#43463) and generative_scoring are output-side shortcuts — neither avoids the full-vocab MatMul, which dominates single-step scoring latency on a single card. Ineligible waves fall back to native, unchanged. Two-level opt-in: engine flag --target-token-scoring + per-request target_token_scoring_normalization="target_set" (default "full_vocab" = existing behavior; logprob_token_ids alone never triggers the compact path, so the flag can't silently change existing logprobs semantics). title: Lightweight vLLM Render API: Offload Heavy Multimodal Preprocessing from CPU Sidecars
body: Problem Statement In the current vLLM architecture, the render API (online_renderer.py -> renderer.render_chat_async -> _process_multimodal -> mm_processor.apply) handles everything from prompt template rendering to heavy multimodal processing. The execution pipeline currently performs the following steps inside apply(): | Step | What happens | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | | Chat template | Messages rendered to a prompt string | Text only | | Media fetch + decode | URLs resolved, images/audio/video decoded | Network + CPU | | Item hashing | Per-item hash derived from the raw media, or a caller-supplied `uuid` | Keys the processor cache and the EC cache | | HF processor | Resize, normalize, patchify; produces `pixel_values`, `image_grid_thw`, … | The expensive step, Heavy CPU bound when having Multimodal Content | | Placeholder expansion | The single `<image>` token is replaced by N placeholder tokens | `_maybe_apply_prompt_updates` | | Placeholder extraction | `PlaceholderRange(offset, length, is_embed)` per item | Derived from the step above | While this works well for text-only workloads, running heavy Hugging Face processor pipelines (resizing, normalization, patchification, and tensor generation—especially for video and audio) inside the render API introduces severe CPU bottlenecks. Proposed Solution & Architecture 1. The vLLM render API should be lightweight and designed to run efficiently on lightweight CPU nodes. This is important for token-in/token-out 2. Lightweight MM Metadata Extraction (Ideal): Explore the feasibility of deriving token placeholder positions purely from media headers and dimensions (e.g., image/video resolution metadata) without executing the full HF image transformation pipeline. 3. GPU Offloading: Any heavy tensor-producing work (e.g., producing pixel_values) should be deferred or offloaded to the GPU worker pool in further phrases like encode stage rather than burdening the CPU-bound routing/rendering layer. _No response_ _No response_

title: Fast Start For vLLM
body: Fast Start reduces vLLM startup time by avoiding repeated checkpoint loading, weight processing, and kernel autotuning during engine restarts and scaling events. The core design uses a persistent per-GPU weight daemon. The daemon loads and processes model weights once, keeps sharded weights in GPU memory, and exposes them to new vLLM engines through CUDA IPC or a multi-node transport. When a compatible cache is unavailable, vLLM falls back to the existing checkpoint loader. - Reuse processed GPU weights across engine instances. - Support TP, PP, EP, multi-node deployments, and MTP. - Support quantized formats including FP8 and FP4. - Cache autotune results with hardware- and version-aware keys. - Preserve correctness through strict cache validation. - Provide a reliable fallback path for cache misses and failures. Cache entries are identified using model and checkpoint identity, quantization configuration, parallelism settings, GPU architecture, vLLM protocol version, and other relevant runtime metadata. Incompatible entries must never be silently reused. Cache misses, stale daemon connections, and validation failures produce diagnostics and fall back to the normal loading path when enabled. - lazy heavy imports (e.g. `torch._inductor`, which `vllm.env_override` imports eagerly); - no GPU queries at import time; - `fork` for workers when the parent has not initialized CUDA; - longer term, a warm "zygote" process kept by the daemon. - Daemon and engine in one container: CUDA IPC needs the same visible GPUs. - Persistent cache directories keyed by version. - The expected behavior for each failure mode. - Warm engine startup avoids repeated checkpoint loading. - Cached and regular loading produce equivalent model outputs. - Cache failures do not compromise correctness or availability. - Startup, cache-hit, fallback, transfer, and autotune timings are observable. _No response_ _No response_

title: KV cache events — bind-time ephemeral port allocation and a discovery API
body: Follow-up to #51275 (Race-free port management). KV cache events are currently classified there as "Category IV: static configured endpoints". This proposal applies the RFC's governing rule — *the process that binds chooses the port at bind time, and publishes the actual endpoint over an existing control path* — to the KV-events publisher, and adds the missing discovery path. Today a consumer of KV events across data-parallel ranks has no race-free way to know where each rank's publisher landed: - `KVEventsConfig.endpoint` requires an explicit port; the DP offset is arithmetic (`base_port + dp_rank`, `vllm/distributed/kv_events.py::offset_endpoint_port`). This is exactly the Category IV static formula: two deployments launched with the same base collide, and passing `tcp://*:0` degenerates to literal ports 0,1,2,... — rank ≥ 1 binds privileged/invalid ports. - `ZmqEventPublisher._socket_setup()` binds the socket but never reads back the assigned port (`zmq.LAST_ENDPOINT`), so with `:0` the OS-assigned port is silently discarded and `get_publisher_config()` still reports the pre-bind wildcard string. - `EngineCoreReadyResponse.kv_events_config` already carries the publisher config to the frontend, but `_apply_ready_response()` discards it; only the Rust gRPC `GetKvEventSources` consumes it, and it receives the unbound wildcard string. There is no Python/HTTP query surface. 1. **Bind-time allocation**: when the configured port is `0`, do not apply the DP offset — each rank's publisher binds `tcp://*:0` independently and the OS hands out distinct ephemeral ports. Explicit non-zero ports keep the existing `base + rank` behavior (backward compatible). 2. **Endpoint readback**: after `bind()`, read `zmq.LAST_ENDPOINT` (for pub and replay sockets), resolve `*` to a reachable host, and update `get_publisher_config()` to return the real bound endpoint. This is the #51275 "final binder reports its endpoint" pattern; the bind itself is the reservation, so there is no probe-the

title: Add --gguf-dequant-on-load option to unlock cuBLAS tensor cores for prefill-heavy workloads`
body: `vllm_gguf_plugin` is popular for running quantized GGUF weights. During autoregressive decoding ($N=1$), memory bandwidth is the bottleneck, and on-the-fly dequantization (`ops.ggml_mul_mat_a8`) is fast. However, for prefill-heavy workloads (such as long-context prompts, batch embeddings, or dataset scoring on $T=8,192$), linear projections are **compute-bound**. On an RTX 4090 running Llama-3.1-8B-Q8_0 on an 8,192-token prompt: - `ggml_mul_mat_a8` takes **~18.2 ms per GEMM** ➔ **15.03 seconds** total model forward pass. - Native `bfloat16` cuBLAS tensor cores take **~1.7 ms per GEMM** ➔ **1.18 seconds** total model forward pass (**12.7x speedup**). Add an optional flag `VLLM_GGUF_DEQUANT_ON_LOAD=1` or `--gguf-dequant-on-load`. When set, the GGUF loader converts Q8_0 (or other compatible formats) to `torch.bfloat16` during model initialization: Users with enough VRAM to hold the unquantized weights (e.g. 16 GB for 8B on a 24 GB card) can immediately benefit from native cuBLAS tensor cores without having to convert GGUF files back to HuggingFace safetensors on disk. --- I searched out a bug and a couple performance optimizations while doing some research. I had the option of not doing anything, or having the LLM write the text. I hope that doesn't bother anyone. The bug was confirmed in another bug post, I added context / appended to the other bug report in terms of fixing it / root cause I determined. _No response_ Test environment as per collect_env

title: Zero-Copy In-Place KV-Cache Compactor via In-Situ Cycle Permutations (1.65x Speedup, 0 Bytes Aux VRAM)
body: In long-context LLM serving (32k to 128k+ tokens), dynamic KV-cache eviction/compaction algorithms (e.g., H2O, Scissorhands, StreamingLLM, or heavy-hitter pruning) are essential to prevent out-of-memory (OOM) faults. However, standard runtimes execute compaction using **out-of-place gathering** (`torch.gather` / dynamic tensor allocation): 1. **Auxiliary VRAM Spikes:** Allocating auxiliary buffers ($O(N \cdot D)$) triggers transient OOM faults during peak concurrency. 2. **HBM Memory Bus Saturation:** Double-buffering incurs redundant read/write transactions across the GPU memory bus. 3. **OS Allocation Latency Jitter:** Dynamic `cudaMalloc` calls introduce unpredictable serving latency spikes and degrade Time-To-First-Token (TTFT). We propose an in-situ idempotent permutation engine (`idempotent-kv`) implemented in OpenAI Triton that reorganizes multi-dimensional KV tensors **directly within existing HBM allocations** using **$O(1)$ scalar hardware registers**: - **Idempotent Invariant:** Enforces $f(f(x)) = f(x)$, locking retained active tokens into stabilized contiguous memory $[0, K-1]$. - **In-Register 2-Cycle Fast-Path:** Mutually transposed tokens are swapped directly within thread registers. - **Bitmask-Free Cycle Follower:** Detects cycle leaders on-the-fly via minimal index traversal, requiring 0 bytes of auxiliary index memory. - **100% Zero Auxiliary VRAM:** Exactly **0.00 MB** secondary global memory allocated. - **Bit-Exact Numerical Parity:** Zero approximation error ($\Delta = 0.000000$, 0 NaN). *Workload: Batch=1, Heads=32, SeqLen=8,192, HeadDim=128, Capacity=4,096 (50% Eviction, float16)* | Implementation | Latency (ms) | Peak Aux VRAM | VRAM Saved | Numerical Diff | | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | | **PyTorch Out-of-Place** | 3.350 ms | 96.00 MB | Baseline | Reference | | **`idempotent-kv` (In-Situ)** | **2.031 ms** | **0.00 MB** | **96.00 MB (100% Saved)** | **0.000000 (Bit-Exact)** | | **Improvement** | **1.65x Faster** | **0.00 MB** |

title: Validate hash-only decode requests in token-in/token-out protocol
body: The `token_in_token_out` `GenerateRequest` protocol currently accepts metadata-only multimodal requests (`features.kwargs_data is None`) with **no validation**. The generate worker silently constructs `mm_kwargs[modality] = [None] * len(hashes)` and forwards the request to the engine, which then fails downstream as an opaque `GenerationError` or `MultiModalCacheMissError` — depending on whether the item happens to be in the local cache. This is a correctness gap. A metadata-only request is legal in exactly two scenarios: 1. **Local cache hit** — the receiver's multimodal cache holds the items. A miss raises `MultiModalCacheMissError` (retryable, self-healing). 2. **Hash-only decode with remote prefill** — `kv_transfer_params` or `ec_transfer_params` signals that multimodal embeddings arrive out-of-band via the encoder-cache connector, so neither tensor data nor a local cache hit is expected. Without either transfer parameter, a metadata-only request is ambiguous: the generate worker has no way to resolve embeddings. Today it is accepted silently and fails late. **Proposed change:** add a `model_validator` on `GenerateRequest` that rejects `features.kwargs_data is None` when neither `kv_transfer_params` nor `ec_transfer_params` is set, with an actionable error message telling the caller exactly what to fix. This is a strict tightening — all currently-legal requests remain legal. The validator only catches requests that would have failed downstream anyway, but earlier and with a clear message. 1. **Do nothing (status quo).** Invalid requests fail as `MultiModalCacheMissError` or `GenerationError` deep in the engine. The error message does not mention `kv_transfer_params` or `ec_transfer_params`, so the caller has no way to know the fix. 2. **Validate in `serving.py` instead of the protocol.** Possible, but protocol-layer validation catches the error before any engine interaction and is testable without a running server. The validator is a focused protocol-layer guard

title: Restart Lifecycle Hooks for KV Transfer Connectors (NIXL)
body: Snapshot/Restore adapters generally require to dispose/reset/reinitialized on warm boot. KV-transfer connectors own transport resources that may need to be rebuilt during snapshot restore, device recovery, or planned transport restart. Currently the connector interface (`KVConnectorBase_V1`) has no way to drain transfers, release transport state, re-register existing KV caches, or verify readiness. We propose to add three connector lifecycle hooks: - `quiesce(timeout)` drains transfers and releases connector-owned transport resources while retaining KV-cache tensors; - `reinitialize()` creates fresh transport state and re-registers the retained caches; and - `verify()` validates local readiness before inference resumes. The base implementation is a no-op for compatibility. `MultiConnector` forwards the hooks to its configured children. NIXL implements the lifecycle, including rebuilding the state needed for peer handshakes. - Recreating the complete worker; but that would unnecessarily discard KV-cache tensors and unrelated worker state. - Adding NIXL-specific operations to the engine; it would couple the engine to one connector implementation. - We temporarily worked around the limitations by monkey-patching the engine, which is undesirable for obvious reasons This change defines the connector-side lifecycle boundary only. It does not define a snapshot format, external suspend/resume API, device recovery policy, or retry policy. The external lifecycle coordinator is responsible for serializing these calls and preventing new transfer work while quiescing. - NIXL pipeline-parallel support: #52913 - CUDA checkpoint/restore: #34303 - Container snapshot suspend/restore: #54940 - Restore implementation work: #54943 - llm-d snapshot orchestrator: llm-d/llm-d#2365 - NIXL stale-peer restart failure: #49238 - NIXL non-terminal transfer failure: #49528

title: Let `vllm launch render` / `--tokens-only` override an inherited `VLLM_ENABLE_SCALE_OUT_ENDPOINTS=0` instead of failing startup
body: Fail-closed is the right approach. A server that starts without any render routes would still pass its health check, only to return 404s for every request. That makes the problem much harder to diagnose. The problem is where the `0` comes from in practice. In llm-d / Dynamo-style deployments, `VLLM_ENABLE_SCALE_OUT_ENDPOINTS=0` is exactly the kind of value a platform or security team sets once as a cluster or namespace wide default. It could be a Helm global, a chart level `env` block or a namespace level pod default. That value is then inherited by every vLLM pod in the namespace including the render and `--tokens-only` pods and every one of them lands in `CrashLoopBackOff` at startup. Two things make this worse than a normal misconfiguration: 1. This unfortunately covers both halves of a disaggregated deployment. The check applies to `vllm launch render` and `vllm serve --tokens-only`, so a single inherited default takes down the renderer pods and the token-in/token-out engine pods together. 2. The person who sets the default is usually not the person who writes the pod spec. A platform team hardening a namespace has no reason to know that two specific launch commands treat the variable as fatal rather than as a default. The current guidance is to "unset it or set it to 1" but unsetting is not available in the configurations above. You cannot remove an env var injected by a namespace default or a Helm global from a downstream pod spec. You can only override it with another value. So the only workable remedy today is "every render and `--tokens-only` pod must set `VLLM_ENABLE_SCALE_OUT_ENDPOINTS=1` explicitly" and that requirement is not stated anywhere. There is also a precedence question worth settling on its own merits. `vllm launch render` is a command explicitly for disaggregated deployment. The env var should not affect this command. Make the explicit launch mode always start: - `vllm launch render` and `vllm serve --tokens-only` register their required endpo
label: feature request

title: Support Sentence Transformers Transformer-Pooling-Dense CrossEncoders
body: Sentence Transformers can save CrossEncoders as explicit module chains. The standard layouts include: - `Transformer` for sequence classification - `Transformer → LogitScore` for causal-LM rerankers - `Transformer → Pooling → Dense` for a feature-extraction backbone with a trained scoring head The first layout already maps to vLLM's sequence-classification path, and vLLM has model-specific support for some causal-LM rerankers. The remaining gap is that vLLM does not interpret the saved Sentence Transformers module stack and its configs. An immediate use case is a multimodal cross-encoder reranker saved as `Transformer → Pooling → Dense`. The Dense layer contains trained checkpoint weights, while the Pooling and Transformer configs define how hidden states and structured multimodal pairs are processed. Sentence Transformers can reload the complete model, but vLLM currently cannot discover the scoring head or reproduce those saved semantics without model-specific code or launch-time overrides. This issue proposes bounded support for the standard serialized layout, starting with the exact `Transformer → Pooling → Dense` chain: - read the CrossEncoder and module metadata saved with the checkpoint - map supported pooling modes to vLLM's pooling runner - load the trained Dense scoring head and its activation - preserve supported structured multimodal input formatting - fail clearly when the checkpoint uses unsupported modules or semantics - leave non-pooled CrossEncoders on their existing vLLM paths This would let the same checkpoint load in Sentence Transformers and vLLM without `trust_remote_code` or a model-specific vLLM implementation. - Add a model-specific sequence-classification implementation in Transformers. This makes the checkpoint portable to Transformers, but fixes the pooling and scoring design at the model-class boundary and requires upstream support for each model family. - Add another model-specific reranker path in vLLM. title: Tokenized Prompt as Input for Chat and Messages Endpoints when serving
body: It would be useful for vLLM HTTP serving endpoints such as `/v1/chat/completions` and `/v1/messages` to accept prompt token IDs as input and skip repeated tokenization, while still preserving normal handling for tools, reasoning, and multimodal content. The concrete examples below focus on `/v1/chat/completions`, but the same need also applies to agent-style message APIs. This is related to the earlier feature request in [vLLM issue #25051](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/25051) (Stale, closed, and maybe outdated). The main goal is simple: if a frontend already has prompt token IDs, vLLM's HTTP chat/message endpoint should be able to consume those IDs directly and skip tokenization. For example, an HTTP routing layer such as vLLM Router may tokenize requests before forwarding them to workers so it can reuse repeated prompt prefixes, estimate prefill cost, or make cache-aware scheduling decisions. If `/v1/chat/completions` cannot accept those token IDs, vLLM has to apply the chat template and tokenize again. Current flow: Desired flow: For pure completion-style requests, vLLM already supports this pattern. `/v1/completions` can accept token IDs through the `prompt` field: Offline and lower-level generation paths also support token-ID-style inputs. Internally, tokenized multimodal inputs are represented as token IDs plus separate multimodal payload fields, not as token IDs alone. For chat-style endpoints, however, users currently cannot cleanly provide the already-tokenized chat prompt through the OpenAI-compatible HTTP API. This blocks tokenization-cache reuse at the HTTP frontend layer and can cause duplicate work: 1. A frontend applies the chat template and tokenizes the prompt for tokenization-cache reuse or scheduling/cache logic. 2. vLLM receives the original chat request and applies the chat template/tokenizes again. title: Add explicit cache IDs for reusable multimodal and inference state
body: There are already several caching mechanisms in vLLM, including multimodal processing/encoder caching and prefix caching. It would be useful to expose an explicit, application-level cache_id (or similar handle) for reusable cached state. The idea is simple: an application sends a large context or image once, vLLM performs the expensive processing and returns a cache_id. Subsequent requests could reference that ID instead of sending and processing the same data again. For example: large document / image ↓ process once ↓ cache_id ↓ question 1 question 2 question 3 ... The handle would be implementation-independent: it could refer to multimodal/vision state, prefix/KV state, or other expensive intermediate state. This would be particularly useful for workloads where the same document or image is queried many times, such as RAG, document analysis, multimodal agents, and batch processing. The main goal is to let applications explicitly retain and reuse expensive computation, rather than relying only on automatic cache matching. The existing automatic prefix caching and multimodal UUID mechanisms are useful, but they still require the application to work with the specific caching mechanism. An explicit cache_id would provide a simple, unified application-level handle while allowing vLLM to decide internally what representation is stored and how it is managed. _No response_

title: Entropy-Gated Dynamic Speculative Decoding (Dynamic k in {0, K}) via Real-Time Shannon Hysteresis
body: Standard speculative decoding in vLLM operates with a static draft length ($k = \text{constant}$). However, during high-entropy generation steps (e.g., complex reasoning forks, multi-lingual syntax, or high-perplexity code tokens), the token acceptance rate $\beta \to 0$. This leads to frequent draft rejection rollbacks, net throughput degradation ($S < 1$), and wasted compute FLOPs/energy. We propose an **Entropy-Gated Stochastic Speculative Controller** that evaluates output distribution Shannon entropy $H(t)$ in real-time and dynamically modulates the draft window: - **$k = K$ (e.g., 5)** during low-entropy deterministic spans (~100% draft acceptance). - **$k = 0$ (single-step fallback)** during high-entropy cognitive search forks, completely eliminating wasted draft passes. To prevent rapid mode-thrashing (gear hunting) on borderline tokens, the controller uses an industrial **Schmitt-trigger hysteresis loop** with EMA smoothing ($\alpha = 0.35$). --- 1. **Numerically Stable Float32 Shannon Entropy:** $$\log p_i = \text{LogSoftmax}(z_i) = z_i - \log \sum_{j \in \mathcal{V}} e^{z_j}$$ $$H(X) = - \frac{1}{\ln 2} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{V}} e^{\log p_i} \cdot \log p_i$$ 2. **Hysteresis State Transitions:** $$ \bar{H}_t = \alpha \cdot H(p_t) + (1 - \alpha) \cdot \bar{H}_{t-1} $$ $$ k_t = \begin{cases} 0, & \text{if } S_{t-1} = \text{Active} \land \bar{H}_t > \theta_{\text{high}} \\ K, & \text{if } S_{t-1} = \text{Fallback} \land \bar{H}_t < \theta_{\text{low}} \\ k_{t-1}, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} $$ *(Default baseline thresholds: θ_low = 0.55 bits, θ_high = 1.25 bits).* --- We benchmarked this control mechanism on Llama-3.1-8B under 100 Hz NVML hardware power polling: - **Electrical Energy per Token:** Reduced by **46.7%** ($6.40\text{ J} \to 3.41\text{ J/token}$). - **Throughput:** Maintained **50.52 tok/s** on complex poetic generation (409 generation steps). - **Draft Rejection Waste:** The clutch successfully locked at $k=5$ for 150+ continuous steps during d

title: Per-request and per-session KV cache tier attribution in OpenTelemetry traces
body: When running hierarchical KV cache tiering (GPU -> CPU -> filesystem via `TieringOffloadingSpec`), operators have no way to trace a single request or session and see which tier served its cached blocks or how long promotion took. The existing `llm_request` OTel span only includes latency and token count attributes. Aggregate per-tier Prometheus metrics exist (`block_hits`, `block_queries`, `read_time` by tier label), but they cannot answer: "Did this specific slow request hit the filesystem tier, and how long did promotion take?" or "How are tier hits distributed across requests in this agentic session?" **Proposal:** Add per-request KV cache tier attribution as span attributes on the existing `llm_request` OTel span. When tiering is enabled and tracing is active, the span would include attributes such as: - `kv_cache.request_id` : the request ID - `kv_cache.session_id` : the session ID, if set (already available on requests via #48048) - `kv_cache.tier_hit` : which tier(s) served cached blocks (e.g., `cpu`, `fs`, `none`) - `kv_cache.blocks_hit` : number of blocks served from cache, by tier - `kv_cache.blocks_missed` : number of blocks that required recomputation - `kv_cache.promotion_latency_seconds` : total promotion time from secondary tier to primary, if applicable Including `session_id` enables operators to filter traces by session, making this useful for agentic workloads where multiple requests share KV cache state within a conversation. This aligns with the session-centric KV cache orchestration direction proposed in RFC #48501. `TieringMetricsTracker` already tracks per-request lookup state internally (`_request_states` dict keyed by `req_id`), including which tier each block resolved at. However, this data is aggregated into counters and the per-request identity is lost at stats collection time. The implementation would extend this existing state to surface a per-request summary through the stats pipeline into the OTel span. - **Structured logging**: Emit

title: Rust frontend: /v1/embeddings endpoint
body: Right now, with VLLM_USE_RUST_FRONTEND=1, hitting /v1/embeddings just returns a 404 Not Found. For example, a simple curl like this: gets back a `404` with an empty body. So the endpoint simply isn't there – you can't use embeddings at all with the Rust frontend enabled, and you're forced to fall back to the Python version. That's the pain point this PR fixes. We're adding `/v1/embeddings` support to the Rust frontend. It handles text and token inputs, batched requests, float/base64 encoding, the dimensions param, LoRA adapters, and usage reporting – fully OpenAI-compatible. Right now the Rust frontend doesn't support embeddings, but a lot of common use cases (RAG, semantic search, classification) need it. If you enable the Rust frontend with VLLM_USE_RUST_FRONTEND=1, you can't use embeddings and have to switch back to the Python frontend – which is a pain. Adding this endpoint makes the Rust frontend actually usable for embedding workloads. This is explicitly listed in the Rust frontend feature parity roadmap (#44280) under "Pooling / embedding APIs". We already have PR #53736 ready. Once merged, we're one step closer to making the Rust frontend the default option. We already have PR https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53736 ready

title: Enable varlen for GLM-5.x/DSV3.2 (Sparse MLA)
body: Adaptive verification has a firm requirement that the attention backend must not use the CPU-side query lengths as a source-of-truth, instead using the GPU tensors (so that we can run the confidence-based assignment on the GPU without synchronizing the CPU). title: Support per-request dynamic LoRA scale
body: Currently `LoRARequest.lora_scale` is fixed at request creation and baked into the CUDA graph / kernel as a scalar. This prevents: - same-adapter requests in one batch from using different strengths; - adjusting LoRA strength mid-generation. A real ASR service works around this by baking scale into separate adapter copies (one slot per scale). This wastes slots and limits scale to discrete presets. **Proposal:** Add `LoRAScaleState` — a per-request `UvaBackedTensor` (`[max_num_reqs]`) following `SamplingStates`, passed to the LoRA kernel along with `token_to_req`. Effective scale = `base_scale * request_lora_scales[token_to_req[token_idx]]`. No per-token memory, CUDA-graph-compatible. **Evaluation (real adapter + WER A/B):** | Condition | CN mean \|B-A\| | EN mean \|B-A\| | | --- | --- | --- | | off (noise floor) | 0.022% | — | | 1.0 pre-fix | 17.184% | — | | 1.0 post-fix | 0.038% | 0.028% | - 4 adapter slots → 1 slot. - Arbitrary continuous scale values. - Two bugs found & fixed: CUDA graph captured the scale-free kernel variant (`tl.constexpr`), and the all-ones buffer wasn't refreshed. - **Baking scale into separate adapter copies** (current workaround) — consumes one adapter slot per scale, limited to discrete presets such as `LORA_SCALES=0.5,0.7,0.9,1.0`. - **Storing a per-token scale array** — would require more GPU memory (e.g. 128 KB per batch vs 1 KB per request) and does not follow vLLM V1 persistent-batch style. - Full per-test-set breakdowns and logs are available on request. - Happy to open a PR if this direction is reasonable.

title: Low-overhead asynchronous early-exit checks & KV-cache reclamation for Continuous Batching
body: Problem Statement In high-throughput production environments running long-context agent loops or strict JSON-enforcement pipelines, models frequently burn a significant portion of generation cycles on post-plateau tail-tokens (e.g., polite wrappers, redundant formatting) after the core semantic task is complete. While stop_strings and custom LogitsProcessor hooks exist, evaluating them per-step in Python introduces severe bottlenecks: CPU-GPU Sync & GIL Contenter: Per-step synchronous callbacks disrupt the execution loop, create heavy interpreter friction, and degrade throughput at scale (batch size > 64). Even in Python-heavy orchestration stacks, this creates unacceptable micro-lags. KV-Cache Bloat & Fragmentation: Finished or logically complete sequences linger in the active batch until the explicit stop token hits or max tokens are reached, occupying precious blocks in PagedAttention and artificially inflating latency for concurrent requests. An Economic Perspective In high-volume enterprise deployments (e.g., fintech, customer ops, logistics), long-context generation loops routinely burn 20–30% of output tokens on post-plateau tail generation. For enterprise clients processing tens of millions of requests monthly, this translates to hundreds of thousands of dollars in wasted infrastructure costs annually, plus artificial latency inflation due to occupied KV-cache slots. Has anyone in the community tackled token overconsumption and mid-batch memory reclamation from a production-economy standpoint? How are large-scale deployments justifying or mitigating these dead compute cycles today? Proposed Solution Introduce a lightweight, optimized mechanism at the scheduler level to handle dynamic early-exit flags and asynchronous KV-cache recycling without heavy interpreter roundtrips: Allow registering low-overhead termination predicates directly within the vLLM scheduler loop. Provide efficient memory reclamation hooks to instantly free PagedAttention blocks for comple

title: Refactor EPD
body: vLLM has the EPD scaffolding (`vllm/distributed/ec_transfer/`, `ECConnectorBase` with scheduler + worker roles, `ECConnectorFactory`, `ec_transfer_params` in the OpenAI layer, E→PD / E→P→D examples). But **every existing EC connector transfers synchronously and locally**, and the encode → stage → send → release flow is hard-wired to that assumption: - `ECExampleConnector` — `save_caches()` writes a safetensors file to shared disk; the consumer `start_load_caches()` reads it back. Blocking, filesystem-bound. - `ECCPUConnector` — offloads the encoder cache into a CPU mmap region on the same host. Blocking, single-host only. There is **no over-the-wire backend**: the encoder and PD instances must share a filesystem or a host. By contrast the KV path already ships pluggable network transports (`NixlConnector`, `MooncakeConnector`, … in `vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/factory.py`). The EC path needs the same: a refactor that turns the single hard-coded transfer path into a **backend-agnostic pipeline** where new transports plug in cleanly. The core goal is the **refactor** — make the encoder-instance flow backend-agnostic so that supporting many transfer backends is a matter of implementing a delivery interface, not rewriting the pipeline. The first two backends to land on top of it: 1. **`ECZmqConnector`** — producer pushes the embedding over a ZMQ socket to the consumer (PD scheduler). Simple, dependency-light, works across nodes. 2. **`ECMooncakeConnector`** — RDMA transfer: the consumer registers a landing buffer and reads the embedding out of the producer's GPU buffer. High throughput for large embeddings. These backends are **asynchronous** and **cross-process**, which the current blocking `save_caches` / `start_load_caches` contract cannot express safely. The refactor exists precisely to make async, over-the-wire transfer correct — and to make the *next* backend after these two trivial to add. Everything after `receive` should follow a single chain, so

title: split local/external prefix-cache hits in `prompt_tokens_details`
body: With distributed prefix caching (KV connectors such as Mooncake / lmcache), cache hits in a single prefill can come from two different sources: - **local**: hits on this instance's GPU prefix cache; - **external**: hits fetched from a remote KV store / another instance via the KV connector. The scheduler already tracks `num_local_cached_tokens` / `num_external_cached_tokens` separately in `PrefillStats`, but `OutputProcessor` only forwards their sum (`num_cached_tokens`), so the breakdown is lost before it reaches the OpenAI serving layer — users cannot tell, per request, where cache hits came from. Exposing this information per-request may also be handy for pricing purposes. With `--enable-prompt-tokens-details` enabled, the response currently looks like: Add two optional keys, `local_cached_tokens` / `external_cached_tokens`, alongside the existing fields: Invariant: `cached_tokens == local_cached_tokens + external_cached_tokens`. - Strictly additive change: existing fields (`cached_tokens` / `created_cache_tokens` / `multimodal_tokens`) must be preserved untouched; - New fields default to `None` and must not affect existing output when the flag is off or the values carry no meaning; - Cover both streaming and non-streaming paths for chat and completion endpoints, and also benefit offline `LLM()` users. _No response_ _No response_

title: Parse Request Priority from HTTP Header
body: As part of company ops, being able to adjust the request priority at an intermediate proxy/load balancer by changing/setting a HTTP header makes it an order of magnitude easier than having to use more specialized tooling to parse the entire request and modify JSON structure. Suggestion: `X-Vllm-Priority` Priority from a header must override any priority found in the request body. The information about the intended priority of requests is often neither of concern, nor even available to individual clients where requests originate. Priority could also change arbitrarily due to ops requirements or business decisions, potentially affecting many clients, which would all have to be reconfigured/reloaded in their own way. A workaround would be having a more complex proxy that is specific to LLM APIs and implements this adjustment or generic enough to offer facilities for manipulating requests. It would need to wait for the entire JSON request, set the field and then pass the request on. For processing of large chats or especially attached files/images, requests can become large, resulting in a lot of overhead and delay on any proxy. _No response_

title: Emit BlockInactive KV events when GPU block ref_cnt drops to zero
body: Add a new KV cache event type, `BlockInactive`, published when a GPU prefix-cached block's `ref_cnt` drops from 1 to 0 in `BlockPool.free_blocks()`. This is distinct from existing events: - `BlockStored`: block becomes actively referenced / stored - `BlockRemoved`: block is physically evicted from memory - `BlockInactive` (proposed): block still resides in GPU memory, but no request currently references it In PD-disaggregated serving, an external scheduler (e.g. a KV-aware router / load balancer) may track per-decode-worker active KV occupancy for decode-node selection, for example: load_score = (query_block_len - overlap_depth) + active_blocks Today, consumers can observe BlockStored / BlockRemoved, but they cannot reliably detect that the last request released a block while it may still sit in the prefix cache. Without a refcount-zero signal, active_blocks tends to only increase, or requires fragile heuristics. I'm working on decode-affinity routing for PD clusters and need a clean, engine-native signal for "GPU block is no longer actively referenced." In BlockPool.free_blocks(), when ref_cnt == 0, enable_kv_cache_events is on, and the block has a hash, append BlockInactive(block_hashes=..., medium=MEDIUM_GPU). Publish via the existing KV event path (ZMQ / take_events()). No new scheduler-loop wiring. Role gate: Prefill-only instances (kv_role == "kv_producer") still emit BlockStored / BlockRemoved, but do not emit BlockInactive, so Prefill frees do not pollute decode load signals. Decode (kv_consumer), union (kv_both), and non-PD setups continue to emit Inactive. Gate with kv_role != "kv_producer" (do not use is_kv_producer, which includes kv_both). Rough mapping to ref_cnt: 0 -> 1 BlockStored N -> N+/-1 (>0) (no new event) 1 -> 0 BlockInactive (proposed) eviction BlockRemoved (unchanged) I have a draft implementation on a fork and can open a PR after discussion. It adds BlockInactive in kv_events.py, gates emission via KVTransferConfig.should_emit_block_inactive

For models with expensive startup phases, this can leave the service unreachable for a long time even though the process is alive and making progress. For example, startup may include: Loading model checkpoints Compiling execution paths Allocating KV cache FlashInfer or backend autotuning CUDA graph capture Model-specific kernel warmup With large or hybrid models, these phases can take many minutes. title: Add DFly speculative decoding and D-Cut support
body: We would like to propose adding DFly speculative decoding support to vLLM, together with D-Cut, a dynamic draft pruning method for speculative decoding. DFly is the main speculative decoding method in this proposal. Existing DFlash/DSpark-style paths are treated as baselines or compatibility foundations. The primary goal is to make DFly usable in vLLM's standard serving stack and improve its runtime efficiency with D-Cut. This proposal focuses on two main features: DFly is a speculative decoding method that uses a draft model to generate candidate tokens for the target model to verify. The proposed integration adds support for running DFly-style draft models inside vLLM, including: - recognizing DFly draft model architectures - registering the DFly draft model implementation - routing DFly through the speculative decoding runtime - supporting the required draft-token transport and verification flow - keeping compatibility with existing speculative decoding infrastructure The expected result is that users can serve target models with a DFly draft model through normal vLLM APIs, without relying on an external or out-of-tree runtime. D-Cut is a dynamic pruning strategy for speculative decoding. Instead of always verifying a fixed number of draft tokens, D-Cut chooses how many draft tokens to keep for each request based on draft confidence and runtime cost. This helps avoid wasting verification compute on low-confidence draft tokens. At a high level, D-Cut provides: - per-request dynamic keep-length selection - confidence-based draft pruning - scheduler-side truncation of draft tokens - keep-ratio metrics - optional cost-aware automatic mode - integration with the DFly speculative decoding path D-Cut is intended to improve the efficiency of DFly by adapting the verification width to each request. Speculative decoding performance depends heavily on both draft quality and verification cost. A fixed draft length can be suboptimal: - if the draft model is confident, verifyi

title: Balanced MoE routing between GPUs
body: With expert parallelism each EP rank owns an equal number of experts. As tokens get routed to the experts, the MoE computations are bottlenecked by the rank that receives the most tokens. I developed a patch that routes tokens to the experts in a balanced way so that each GPU rank gets approximately equal number of tokens. This increases performance significantly (see the benchmark table below). As a result, a given token might not always get the best possible expert, but rather it gets routed to the best available (under loaded) expert. This might affect the accuracy slightly, but we can adjust the intensity of the feature by a "capacity_factor" that enables us to control the tradeoff between performance and accuracy. In the future we could also introduce redundant experts that may allow us to eliminate the accuracy regression completely. Vllm benchmark validation: Image: vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:v0.25.1 Model: deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3 ISL: 4096 OSL: 256 max_concurrency: 128 | MOE_balancing | Capacity_factor | Requests/s | Tokens/s | TTFT | TPOT | gsm8k accuracy| |---------------|-----------------|-----|----------|------|------|-------| | Off | inf | 3.23 | 14060 | 1780 | 143 | 95.07 | | On | 1.5 | 3.38 | 14712 | 1678 | 137 | 94.84 | | On | 1.2 | 3.46 | 15036 | 1629 | 134 | 93.33 | All comments and ideas regarding this topic are welcome. We were also looking into the Expert Parallelism Load Balancer (EPLB) that was developed in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/18343. However, this feature didn't provide any uplift for our workload, and it was also incompatible with VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_FUSION_SHARED_EXPERTS. title: w8a8_block_int8_matmul kernel is dormant
body: `w8a8_block_int8_matmul` still exists in `vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/utils/int8_utils.py`, but there is no in-tree production dispatch to it in current vLLM main. The former wrapper, `apply_w8a8_block_int8_linear`, was later removed in PR #47329 as unused dead code. The key distinction is that the kernel landed, but the upstream quantization-method integration did not. In contrast, the block-FP8 path is documented and actively supported in vLLM, while current vLLM INT8 support is documented through other W8A8 flows rather than this block-INT8. - PR #13942 was the upstream attempt to add a full `blockwise_int8` integration, including config and dispatch for models such as `meituan/DeepSeek-R1-Block-INT8`, but it never landed. Issue #14176 was a separate request for DeepSeek-R1 block/channel INT8 support and likewise did not produce merged upstream support. - PR #16366 added the Triton-side block-INT8 kernel scaffolding, including `w8a8_block_int8_matmul`, but not a lasting upstream serve path.PR #47329 later removed `apply_w8a8_block_int8_linear`, which is consistent with the absence of any surviving upstream caller. The most accurate current description is: upstream vLLM still contains the block-INT8 GEMM kernel implementation, but not an upstream quantization config or linear-method path that would select it during normal serving. So the code is present but unreachable from mainline model dispatch. Separately, the published vLLM docs show active support for FP8 and other INT8/W8A8 quantization workflows, which should not be conflated with this specific block-INT8 path. vLLM's `_w8a8_block_int8_matmul` body is structurally identical to sglang's `python/sglang/kernels/ops/quantization/int8_kernel.py::_w8a8_block_int8_matmul` Filing to document the state and surface the decision that hasn't been made anywhere in-tree, so it's discoverable next time someonenruns into the gap. title: Integration of HieraSparse N:M Semi-Structured Sparse KV Cache Attention
body: As context lengths scale to 64k–192k+ tokens, TTFT (Time-To-First-Token) and memory footprint become significant bottlenecks in long-context LLM serving. While unstructured pruning drops elements without offering compute speedup, and coarse-grained token/head pruning can degrade model accuracy, modern NVIDIA GPUs (Ampere, Hopper) feature **2:4 N:M sparse tensor cores** that offer up to 2× speedup for sparse GEMMs. Currently, vLLM lacks native support for semi-structured N:M sparse KV cache acceleration using hardware sparse tensor cores. --- We request native integration or an experimental backend feature based on the [HieraSparse architecture](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.16864) ([GitHub Repo](https://github.com/psl-ntu/HieraSparse)). HieraSparse introduces a hierarchical semi-structured sparse attention framework designed for long-context KV cache compression: 1. **Hierarchical Block + Element Masking:** Keeps critical blocks (attention sinks, local context windows) dense while applying $N:M$ semi-structured pruning (e.g., 2:4) to non-critical blocks. 2. **Trans-Both Layout Optimization:** Transposes both attention GEMM stages ($S^T = K \times Q^T$ and $O^T = V^T \times P^T$), positioning offline-pruned $K$ and $V$ matrices as the first operands to directly utilize hardware sparse tensor cores (`mma.sp`). 3. **Paged Memory Compatibility:** Uses a block index mapping scheme with separate non-zero and metadata pools, which aligns closely with vLLM’s existing `PagedAttention` design. --- * **Unstructured Pruning (e.g., MUSTAFAR):** Reduces memory loading bandwidth, but compute remains dense, yielding minimal speedup on compute-bound stages like prefill attention. * **Coarse Token Skipping (e.g., SnapKV, H2O):** Skips entire tokens, which often leads to severe accuracy degradation in complex long-context tasks compared to fine-grained element-level $N:M$ sparsity. --- According to the published paper: * **Speedup:** Achieves up to **1.85× attention speedup in prefill**

title: Plan for enabling mypy in tests directory
body: **Goal:** Enable MyPy static checking in the `/tests` directory. **Implementation:** Move `tests/**` from `--follow-imports skip` to `--follow-imports silent` in [`tools/pre_commit/mypy.py`](../../tools/pre_commit/mypy.py), one directory at a time, **with each PR enforcing the directories it fixed**. Partial: #26533 /cc @hmellor @yewentao256 --- **Note:** Errors below were measured with `mypy --python-version 3.10 --follow-imports silent <dir>` — the target state for each directory. --- `group_files()` iterates `SEPARATE_GROUPS` in **list order** and `break`s on the first prefix match. `"tests"` is the first entry, so every `tests/**` file is claimed by it: A file only gets `follow_imports=silent` by matching **no** entry at all and falling through to the `""` group. Since `"tests"` matches everything under `tests/`, no per-directory removal can ever take effect before `"tests"` itself is removed — which is the very last step. **Sorting `SEPARATE_GROUPS` by longest prefix does not fix this** (verified): with `tests/config` removed, its files still match `tests` and still run with `skip`. Sorting only changes which *skip* group a file lands in, which is cosmetic today. Consequence if the plan is executed as originally written: every PR from 1 through kv-C fixes real errors but enforces none of them, and all of that work is free to regress until the final PR. **PR 0 below fixes the mechanism so that stops being true.** --- Add an allowlist of verified-clean directories, matched **before** `SEPARATE_GROUPS`, that routes files into the `""` group (no `--follow-imports` flag → pyproject's `silent`): In `group_files()`, before the `SEPARATE_GROUPS` loop: Also sort the `SEPARATE_GROUPS` loop by descending path length so sub-directory groups stop being shadowed by their parents. This is cosmetic today (all those groups run at `skip`) but keeps the per-group log labels honest as directories drain. Verified behaviour with `SILENT_GROUPS = ["tests/config", "tests/v1/shutdown"]

title: Real-time request-queue signal (NUM_REQUESTS_RUNNING/WAITING) for external routers
body: I'm working on an external load-balancing router that dispatches across N vLLM engines for RL rollout (the kvc-aware router in [verl](https://github.com/volcengine/verl)), and I'd like a **real-time, low-latency way to read per-engine request-queue state** — `num_requests_running`, `num_requests_waiting`, and ideally a request-lifecycle event stream (admitted → waiting → running → completed) — so the router doesn't have to rely on the Prometheus `/metrics` endpoint, which is seconds stale. This is the specific problem behind it: the router polls `/metrics` to decide where to send each request, but the queue-depth gauges lag reality by seconds, for two stacked reasons — (1) the scrape cadence itself (a 5 s Prometheus poll is typical), and (2) vLLM's own `waiting → running` scheduler transition. We measured it end-to-end on vLLM 0.21.0: at cold start the router's own synchronous inflight counter is non-zero the instant the first request is dispatched, while `num_requests_running`/`num_requests_waiting` stay **0 for ~18 s** (3–4 poll cycles) and then jump to ~18; in steady state running/waiting trail the true dispatch rate by **3–6 s**. For those 18 cold-start seconds the router's overload and queue signals are all 0, so it routes on inflight alone and collapses the first wave onto the first engine; in steady state every routing decision is based on 3–6 s stale depth. **Pitch.** Any of: - a request-lifecycle **event stream** (SSE / WebSocket / gRPC streaming) emitting running/waiting/inflight transitions as they happen, analogous to the existing KV-cache event stream but for request-queue depth; **or** - a dedicated low-latency stats RPC alongside `/metrics` (no Prometheus scrape round-trip / exposition cost); **or at minimum** - a documented primitive so routers can *subscribe* to queue-depth changes instead of polling. Related / adjacent: #49537 (separate problem — KV-cache events emit 0 events for hybrid models — but found while instrumenting the same router against

title: Support KV-cache events & KV-transfer for hybrid-attention models
body: The KV-transfer connector (`--kv-transfer-config`, e.g. mooncake) currently does **not** work for **hybrid-attention** models — models whose `layer_types` mix `full_attention` with `linear_attention` / state-space layers and are flagged `IsHybrid` (e.g. Qwen3.5, which alternates `linear_attention` (GatedDeltaNet) with `full_attention` every 4 layers). It hard-crashes at startup. KV-cache events (`--kv-events-config`), by contrast, **work** for hybrid models on v0.21 (one gotcha around the inflated hybrid `block_size`, noted below). I'm building cache-aware request routing and want to use a KV-transfer connector for KV migration across hybrid-model replicas; the crash blocks that. Matrix (reproduced end-to-end, logs available on request): | vLLM | `--kv-transfer-config` only | `--kv-events-config` only | both | neither (control) | |---|---|---|---|---| | **0.18.0** | 💥 hard crash | 💥 hard crash | 💥 hard crash | ✅ serves | | **0.21.0** | 💥 hard crash | ✅ works (see note below) | 💥 hard crash | ✅ serves | KV-cache events work correctly for hybrid models on v0.21. There is no bug here; this note records one non-obvious behavior so anyone validating hybrid kv-events isn't misled. For an `IsHybrid` model, vLLM aligns the attention page size to be `>=` the mamba page size, which inflates the attention `block_size`. For Qwen3.5-9B this lands at **528 tokens** (log: `Setting attention block size to 528 tokens to ensure that attention page size is >= mamba page size`), vs the standard **16** for a full-attention model. `BlockStored` is emitted only once a full `block_size` worth of tokens is filled (`block_pool.py`, `cache_blocks` path), so: | Model | `layer_types` | attention `block_size` | prompt tokens sent | KV-cache events emitted | |---|---|---|---|---| | `Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507` (standard) | all `full_attention` | 16 | ~48 | **3 × BlockStored** (`group_idx=0`, `block_size=16`) ✅ | | `Qwen3.5-9B` (`IsHybrid`) | `linear_attention` + `full_attention` (interval 4) | **528*

title: Recency-based progressive mixed-precision KV cache
body: I would like to propose a generic recency-based progressive mixed-precision KV cache. Instead of storing the entire KV cache using one uniform format, vLLM would keep recently created KV blocks in a user-selected higher-precision tier and progressively quantize older completed blocks into lower-precision tiers. The feature should **not be hardcoded to BF16 as the highest tier**. The ordered precision policy should be configurable. Examples include: Example percentage-based policies: or, for a cache whose highest selected precision is FP8: New KV entries and the active partially filled tail block would be written into the **first/highest tier selected by the policy**, which may be BF16, FP8, NVFP4, or another supported format. Once a block is complete and crosses a configured age boundary, it could be asynchronously quantized and moved to the next lower-precision pool. This proposal is specifically about using different KV-cache formats **within the same attention layer based on block age**. It is different from layer-wise mixed precision, where different transformer layers use different formats. Long-context KV caches consume a substantial amount of GPU memory. A uniform low-precision KV cache reduces memory usage, but it applies the same precision to recent and old entries. For long-context and agentic workloads, it may be useful to preserve a recent window in the policy's selected highest precision while compressing older context more aggressively. The intended abstraction is not a single special-case mode such as BF16 + FP8 + NVFP4. It is a generic ordered list of storage tiers. For example: - a BF16-based policy can progressively demote blocks into FP8 and NVFP4; - an FP8-based policy can progressively demote blocks into NVFP4; - an NVFP4-based policy could use a future lower-precision storage format when one is supported; - different hardware backends may expose different valid tier combinations. I understand this is likely an edge case given the age of the hardware, but wanted to document the situation in case it's useful for the project — either for improving error messaging or for considering potential kernel tuning. | Item | Value | |---|---| | **vLLM version** | `0.19.1rc1.dev4` | | **Commit** | [`fa9e680`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/fa9e68022d29c5396dfbb96d13587b6bc1bdb933) | | **GPU** | 2× NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 Ti (22 GB, CC 7.5, Turing) | | **CUDA Driver** | 580.126.18, CUDA 13.0 | | **Python** | 3.12 (Docker) | | **Model** | Gemma4-31B AWQ 4-bit (`google/gemma-4-31b-it`), also reproduced with `cyankiwi/gemma-4-31B-it-AWQ-4bit` | Gemma4's `text_config` specifies `head_dim: 256` (sliding attention) and `global_head_dim: 512` (full attention). title: Improve error handling when task='classify' is used with decoder-only models (e.g., Qwen, Llama, Mistral)
body: **Title:** Improve error handling when `task='classify'` is used with decoder-only models (e.g., Qwen, Llama, Mistral) **Body:** When initializing an `LLM` instance with `task='classify'` on a **decoder-only causal language model** (such as `Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct`, `meta-llama/Llama-3-8B`, or `mistralai/Mistral-7B-v0.1`), vLLM fails during model loading with a cryptic error: This occurs because: - The `task='classify'` option triggers the use of a classification head (`score` layer). - However, standard Causal LM checkpoints (like those from Qwen, Llama, Mistral) **do not contain a `score.weight` parameter**, as they are not trained for sequence classification. - vLLM attempts to construct a model with this missing head and only fails at weight-loading time. > Note: Same issue occurs with `meta-llama/Llama-3-8B`, `mistralai/Mistral-7B-v0.1`, etc. vLLM should **validate compatibility between `task` and model architecture early** (e.g., in `LLM.__init__` or engine args parsing) and raise a clear, actionable error such as: Check the model’s architecture before enabling classification mode: Additionally, the documentation for the `task` parameter should explicitly list supported model types. - **vLLM version**: 0.12.0 - **Model**: `Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct` (but affects all Causal LMs) - **Use case**: User mistakenly assumed `task='classify'` works for any model; better guardrails would improve UX. --- Feel free to adjust the tone or add more details, but this version clearly explains the problem, provides reproducible code, proposes a solution, and aligns with vLLM’s goal of being user-friendly and robust. Let me know if you'd like a Chinese version or help submitting it!

title: MoE flatten_tp_size should not unconditionally include dp_size — DP loses its original semantics for MoE layers
body: In FusedMoEParallelConfig.flatten_tp_across_dp_and_pcp (vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/config.py:979-988), when EP is not enabled, dp_size is unconditionally folded into the flattened TP size: This means that for MoE layers, DP no longer behaves as "data parallelism" (independent replicas processing different data). Instead, it becomes an additional weight-sharding dimension — effectively turning DP ranks into extra TP ranks for MoE weights only. I believe this conflates two distinct parallelism concepts and leads to practical deployment issues. Concrete failure case When deploying Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-FP8 (which has intermediate_size=512 for MoE experts): TP=8, DP=1: intermediate_size_per_partition = 512 / 8 = 64, which is smaller than the FP8 block quantization size (128). This causes a quantization alignment error. TP=4, DP=2 (hoping to avoid the above issue): The MoE layer computes flatten_tp_size = 2 * 1 * 4 = 8, so intermediate_size_per_partition = 512 / 8 = 64 — the exact same problem. DP=2 does not help at all because DP is silently absorbed into TP for MoE layers. There is currently no way to deploy this model on 8 GPUs with TP=4 and have MoE layers actually use tp_size=4 (giving intermediate_size_per_partition = 512 / 4 = 128), because the flatten logic always forces MoE to shard across all devices. Semantic concern For non-MoE layers (Attention, Dense MLP), DP ranks hold identical weight replicas and process different batches independently. But for MoE layers (when EP is disabled), DP ranks hold different weight slices and must communicate to produce correct results. This means: - "DP" has fundamentally different meanings for MoE vs. non-MoE layers within the same model, which is confusing. - Users cannot independently control the MoE sharding strategy — it is implicitly determined by dp_size, which was chosen for throughput/batch scheduling reasons, not for MoE weight distribution. - The tight coupling prevents valid deployment configurations (as shown

body: Key facts: vLLM 0.15.1, Qwen3-Coder-Next-FP8, 4×RTX 3090, TP=4 Single tool call request → complete system hard-freeze (requires power cycle) Same request without tools field → works fine at 465 t/s. 50 concurrent simple requests → works fine. Even without --enable-auto-tool-choice / --tool-call-parser, sending requests with tools in the payload freezes the system (because the chat template still processes them) This is a serious bug — it hard-locks the entire machine, not just the vLLM process.
